title: Completion of a strict law defined on a dense open square
statement: Let $A$ be a Noetherian normal strictly henselian local ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-weil-pbc-normal-ring, def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], and put $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Products and fibres are scheme-theoretic base changes [def-pc-base-change]. An open $U\subset Y$ in an $S$-scheme is $S$-dense if $U_s$ is dense in $Y_s$ for every $s\in S$. An $S$-rational map is a morphism on an $S$-dense open, modulo agreement on an $S$-dense common open; an $S$-birational map is represented by an isomorphism between $S$-dense opens. Smoothness and finite type have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]; separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. A strict birational law on a smooth separated finite-type $S$-scheme $Y$ with nonempty fibres is an associative $S$-rational map $m:Y\times_SY\dashrightarrow Y$ for which there are opens $D,V,W\subset Y\times_SY$, each dense in every fibre of both projections to $Y$, such that $m$ is defined on $D$ and $(x,y)\mapsto(x,m(x,y))$, $(x,y)\mapsto(m(x,y),y)$ induce isomorphisms $D\simeq V$ and $D\simeq W$, respectively. Let $Z\to S$ be smooth, separated and of finite type with nonempty fibres, let $n$ be a strict birational law on $Z$, and assume $Z(S)\ne\varnothing$. Suppose that $U\subseteq Z$ is an $S$-dense open and $n$ has a representative on all of $U\times_SU$. Then there are morphisms $\mu:Z\times_SZ\to Z$, $\iota:Z\to Z$ and $e:S\to Z$ extending $n$ and satisfying the associativity, left and right unit, and left and right inverse diagrams. They give a unique $S$-group scheme structure with this rational law. Group schemes mean these group-object diagrams, as in [def-sc-group-scheme] with base $S$.

source.place: 5.3 Lemma 8, printed pp.127-128 (PDF pp.133-134), including the birational-translation functor of 5.2 Lemma 4; primary scan read at https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~kamenova/homepage_files/Bosch_Raynaud_Neron_Model_tc.pdf; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Apply the graph-chart lemma to $(Z,n)$ and write $d(x,y)=x^{-1}y$ for its rational left division. Use the translation embedding $\tau:Z(T)\hookrightarrow B_Z(T)$ for every $S$-scheme $T$. The graph identities give $\tau_{n(x,y)}=\tau_x\tau_y$ and $\tau_{d(x,y)}=\tau_x^{-1}\tau_y$ on the respective maximal domains. All three graph projections are open immersions with images dense in both projection fibres; thus multiplication and division in either variable are birational on those fibres. These facts hold without any group structure on $Z$ yet.

In $Z^3$ with coordinates $(a,b,c)$, let $E$ be the open where $n(b,a)$ and $d(a,c)$ are defined and both lie in $U$. Fix any point $(b,c)$ of $Z^2$. The graph charts, after the residue-field extension at this point, make $a\mapsto n(b,a)$ and $a\mapsto d(a,c)$ birational maps on the fibre. Since $U$ is fibrewise dense, the inverse image of $U$ under each contains a dense open of that fibre. Their intersection is dense and nonempty. Hence $E\to Z^2$, $(a,b,c)\mapsto(b,c)$, is surjective. On $E$ the formula $h=n(n(b,a),d(a,c))$ is a morphism, because its two arguments lie in $U$ and $n$ is given on all of $U^2$. Where $n(b,c)$ is defined, the translation identities give $\tau_h=\tau_b\tau_a(\tau_a^{-1}\tau_c)=\tau_{n(b,c)}$, so injectivity identifies $h$ with the pullback of $n$. The regularity lemma applied to this open-product projection therefore extends $n$ to a morphism $\mu:Z^2\to Z$.

source.place: 5.3 Lemma 8, first paragraph, with the generic-variable formula written out

proof.text: Let $E'\subset Z^3$ be the open where $d(b,a)$ and $d(a,c)$ are both defined. For fixed $(b,c)$ each condition is a dense open condition on $a$ by the two-variable birationality in the graph lemma; their intersection is nonempty. Thus $E'\to Z^2$ is surjective. The map $h'=\mu(d(b,a),d(a,c))$ is now a morphism on all of $E'$. On the common domain with $d(b,c)$, its translation is $(\tau_b^{-1}\tau_a)(\tau_a^{-1}\tau_c)=\tau_b^{-1}\tau_c=\tau_{d(b,c)}$. Injectivity identifies the two representatives. Flat detection along $E'\to Z^2$ gives an everywhere-defined morphism $\delta:Z^2\to Z$ extending $d$. The graph lemma says that its domain is the image of $q_{13}$, so this image is now all of $Z^2$; similarly the image of $q_{12}$ is all of $Z^2$. The translation identities of step 1 consequently hold for $\mu$ and $\delta$ on all $T$-valued pairs, for arbitrary $T$.

source.place: 5.3 Lemma 8, second paragraph: explicit argument for global left division

proof.text: Choose the assumed section $z_0:S\to Z$. Define morphisms $e=\delta(z_0,z_0):S\to Z$ and $\iota(x)=\delta(x,e):Z\to Z$. For every $T$, the identities already obtained yield $\tau_{e_T}=\tau_{z_{0,T}}^{-1}\tau_{z_{0,T}}=1$ and $\tau_{\iota(x)}=\tau_x^{-1}$. Applying injectivity of $\tau$ to $\tau_x\tau_y\tau_z$ proves associativity of $\mu$; applying it to $1\tau_x=\tau_x1=\tau_x$ proves the two unit identities, and to $\tau_x\tau_x^{-1}=\tau_x^{-1}\tau_x=1$ proves the two inverse identities. These are identities on all $T$-valued points, natural in $T$; taking universal points proves the group-object diagrams as identities of scheme morphisms. This constructs the required structure, with the base-$S$ diagrams meant in the statement.

source.place: 5.3 Lemma 8, concluding functor-of-points argument, printed pp.127-128

proof.text: If another group structure has the same rational law, its multiplication and $\mu$ are two everywhere-defined representatives of that law and hence coincide by uniqueness in the regularity lemma. For one fixed multiplication any two unit sections satisfy $e'=\mu(e',e)=e$, and any two two-sided inverses of $x$ satisfy $y=\mu(y,\mu(x,y'))=\mu(\mu(y,x),y')=y'$. Taking universal points gives equality of the unit and inverse morphisms. Thus the $S$-group scheme structure is unique.

source.place: 5.3 Lemma 8; elementary uniqueness of identity and inverse
